hetuvidya:
The Buddhist science of argumentation and of knowledge; the Sanskrit "hetuvidyā" means "the science of reasons" — the enquiry into what sort of reason (hetu) can make an argument hold.

**From five members to three** Early on, under the influence of the Nyāya school, the "five-member formulation" was used (thesis, reason, example, application, conclusion); Dignāga (c. 480–540) changed it into **three members**: the thesis (the proposition to be established), the reason (the ground), and the example (the illustration). For instance: sound is impermanent (thesis); because it is produced (reason); whatever is produced is seen to be impermanent, like a pot (example).

**"The triple mark of the reason"** A reason must satisfy three conditions in order to hold: it must be a property of the subject (the reason genuinely belongs to the object under discussion); it must be present in similar instances (it exists in cases of the same kind); and it must be absent from dissimilar instances (it does not exist in counter-cases). This is the criterion for judging the validity of an argument, and the core of the Buddhist treatment of "logical necessity."

**Direct perception and inference** Dignāga's *Pramāṇasamuccaya* establishes "two means of knowledge": **direct perception** is awareness free of conceptual construction, and **inference** is the cognition arrived at from a reason. Here "conceptual construction" (kalpanā) **refers specifically to the construction of names and concepts, not to "judgement"** — the *Nyāyamukha* explains it as "being far removed from all construction by way of kind, name, imputation, and non-difference," that is, not positing what is perceived as the name-class "blue" or "sound"; direct perception is therefore not "making no judgement," but rather not yet having fallen into conceptual positing. This is the point most easily read backwards. **The distinctive feature of Buddhist pramāṇa theory is that it links epistemology to soteriology** — "knowing things as they are" is precisely [[right_view|right view]], and therefore "what counts as reliable cognition" is not a purely theoretical question.

**Dharmakīrti (c. 7th century)**, in the *Pramāṇavārttika* and the other six of his seven treatises on pramāṇa, argued further for the reliability of the "means of knowledge," and these became the main subject of monastic education in Tibetan Buddhism. On the Chinese side, hetuvidyā was transmitted by Xuanzang and served mainly as **an instrument of debate** rather than an independent discipline, being merely an auxiliary to the doctrine of the Faxiang school — the *Nyāyapraveśa* and Kuiji's *Yinming Dashu* are the principal texts of Chinese hetuvidyā.

One historical fact worth noting: **hetuvidyā declined in the Chinese transmission but became a prominent learning in the Tibetan**. The Tibetan tradition combined pramāṇa theory with [[madhyamaka|Madhyamaka]] ("Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka + pramāṇa") and developed an extremely rigorous education in debate; the Chinese tradition, by contrast, always gave weight to "depending on the teaching to set out on practice." This is one of the clearest divisions between the two Buddhist traditions in methodological preference.
sarvastivada:
The school among the nikāyas with the most systematic philosophy; it holds that "the three times are real and the substance of the dharmas is eternal": the substance of dharmas past, present, and future is all truly existent, and only their function (their activity) arises, has not yet arisen, or has ceased according to time.

This claim is not an arbitrary metaphysical preference but a way of accommodating the fruit of karma: if there were no substance of dharmas in past and future, on what ground would "karma already performed" ripen in a later life? The Sarvāstivāda therefore needs a substance of dharmas that does not disappear when its function ceases. This also explains why it posits at the same time "unmanifest form" (avijñapti-rūpa) — a kind of [[rupa|form]] produced by bodily and verbal karma that is invisible and persists, and that serves to carry the continuity of [[jie_ti|the essence of the precepts]] and of karma.

The doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda (usually taken in the arrangement of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*): the "categories" of the five categories and seventy-five dharmas are five classes: **form dharmas** (matter, eleven) — judged by the criterion of "change and decay, resistance and obstruction"; **mind dharmas** (the mind itself, one) — judged by the criterion of "discernment"; **mental-factor dharmas** (the concomitant activities of mind, forty-six) — judged by the criterion of "arising in association with mind"; **dharmas not associated with mind** (fourteen) — "neither form nor mind, yet not associated with form or mind," such as arising, duration, perishing, acquisition, and non-acquisition; and **unconditioned dharmas** (three) — "not produced by causes and conditions," namely analytical cessation, non-analytical cessation, and space. Their detailed items are as follows (eleven form dharmas, one mind dharma, forty-six mental-factor dharmas, fourteen dharmas not associated with mind, three unconditioned dharmas); the sixteen aspects of the four noble truths; the forty-six mental factors; and the coexistence of the reality of the three times with "perishing in every instant" (the substance of the dharmas is eternal while their function perishes in every instant — the two do not contradict each other).

Historically it was the dominant school of north-western India (Kaśmīra, Gandhāra), and it is at once the direct opponent and the source of Chinese Abhidharma and of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. Chinese scholars often come to know the Sarvāstivāda through the *Kośa*, but the school's own fuller position must be sought in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā* — the two differ on many details and must not be conflated.
paratantra:
All dharmas arise from causes and conditions and appear in dependence on consciousness; this belongs to the level of [[dependent_origination|dependent origination]]. "Dependent on others" (paratantra) means "arising in dependence on other conditions" — not autonomous, not independent, entirely constituted by conditions.

The dependent nature is the pivot among the [[three_natures|three natures]] and also the focus of the most concentrated discussion between Yogācāra and Madhyamaka: Madhyamaka holds that the dependent nature is synonymous with dependent origination, that is, "without intrinsic nature"; Yogācāra, by contrast, diverges from Madhyamaka precisely in acknowledging the dependent nature as **truly existent**. What Yogācāra calls "existence" must be distinguished from "having intrinsic nature": the dependent nature **arises in reliance on a multitude of conditions**, and therefore is not "entirely without any nature" (like an illusion, it is not that the thing does not exist), yet it is also **without independent intrinsic nature** — the two words "dependent on others" themselves already negate intrinsic nature. *Cheng Weishi Lun*, fascicle 8, states: "the substance that is the basis of the two is truly produced in reliance on conditions; this nature is not non-existent, and is named the dependent nature," and fascicle 9 further establishes upon the dependent nature "the absence of intrinsic nature in respect of arising." The dispute between Yogācāra and Madhyamaka therefore does not lie in "existence or non-existence" but in **whether "absence of intrinsic nature" is precisely equivalent to "non-existence"**: Madhyamaka does not allow a "truly existent" to be established apart from the absence of intrinsic nature, whereas Yogācāra does allow it.

Within the Yogācāra system, the dependent nature corresponds directly to "consciousness" — since it appears in dependence on consciousness, the dependent nature is what consciousness transforms.
three_natures:
The structure of delusion and awakening in [[vijnapti_matra|consciousness-only]] (Yogācāra): the [[parikalpita|imagined nature]], the dependent nature, and the perfected nature. The three are not three worlds but three cognitive states with respect to one and the same dependently originated dharma.

Their relation is as follows:
- The dependent nature — all dharmas arise from causes and conditions and appear in dependence on consciousness; this is the actual level of existence;
- The imagined nature — falsely grasping the dharmas of the dependent nature as possessing an independent intrinsic nature; this belongs to "delusion";
- The perfected nature — on the basis of the dependent nature, being free from the imagined nature and realising the suchness revealed by the two emptinesses; this belongs to "awakening."

Hence within the three natures the dependent nature is the pivot: neither delusion nor awakening is apart from it, the difference lying only in whether grasping has arisen upon it. The three correspond to three levels of "existence," and these three terms must first be distinguished: **provisional existence** — established solely upon names and designations, without substantial reality of its own (the imagined nature); **conventional existence** — appearing in dependence on causes and conditions, and not absent within the conventional truth (the dependent nature); **ultimate existence** — true and not deceptive within the ultimate truth (the perfected nature). Hence "the imagined nature belongs to provisional existence" does not conflict with its "being absent in principle": provisional existence just means "having no substance and being merely name." The correspondence with the two truths is: the imagined nature belongs to provisional existence, the dependent nature to conventional existence, and the perfected nature to ultimate existence.

The three natures are also the basis on which the three doors of liberation are established (see *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74); this group of concepts therefore runs through Yogācāra ontology, epistemology, and soteriology at once.
eight_consciousnesses:
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mind-consciousness, manas, and [[alaya|ālaya-consciousness]]. The first six consciousnesses discern coarse objects, manas constantly examines and deliberates, and ālaya-consciousness retains the seeds and receives perfuming.

How the doctrine of the eight consciousnesses came to be established: the first five consciousnesses are sensory cognition; the sixth, mind-consciousness, synthesises and discerns, and also takes past and future as its objects; the seventh, manas, **constantly examines and deliberates**: it takes the seeing aspect of the eighth consciousness as its object and constantly grasps it as "I," so that its nature is "obscured and morally neutral," and it is the direct source of self-grasping (unlike the first six consciousnesses, which have interruptions, it arises at all times); the eighth, ālaya, contains all seeds, becomes manifest when conditions obtain, and performs the function of being the vehicle of the [[continuity|continuity]] of karma.

The significance of this system lies in solving the technical problem of "rebirth without a self": there is no need to posit a substantial soul, yet one must explain how karma continues across lives — ālaya-consciousness performs precisely this function by way of "the continuity of consciousness" rather than "the transmigration of a substance."
